newsitem.title: INDIA: YEAREND - Indian edible oil imports seen on uptrend.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Indian edible oil imports seen on uptrend.

text.p: India, faced with stagnant oilseed yields and crop area, needs to step up edible oil imports progressively to meet growth in demand driven by rising per capita income, trade and industry officials said on Tuesday.
Industry officials said India would need to import nearly 1.5 million tonnes of edible oil in 1996/97 (November-October), despite a marginal rise in oilseeds output.
India imported nearly 1.25 million tonnes of edible oil in 1995/96, out of which one million tonnes was palm olein.

"Unless we achieve a breakthorugh in yields, which is difficult in Indian conditions, we have reached the plateau in oilseeds production," Navinbhai Shah, president of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd, told Reuters.
"We will have to depend on imports, which will go up," Shah said.
"In years to come, imports will go up, to almost two million tonnes by the year 2000," said G.K. Sood, chief executive of the Vanaspati Manufacturers Association of India.
India has doubled its oilseeds production over the past ten years, mainly by expanding the area under the crop.
India's per capita expenditure has been growing at a rate of 10 to 11 percent during the last five years. This implies the demand for edible oils will rise as income grows.
India consumes over seven million tonnes of edible oil a year against a domestic output of nearly 6.2 million. The gap is met through imports.
"During the last 10 to 15 years, the productivity increase is two percent per annum. There is a saturation in area," Sood said.
He said the per capita consumption of edible oil had grown to 9.7 kg in 1996 from 5.0 kg in the 1970s.

According to trade estimates, from 10.8 million tonnes in 1986/87, India reached an oilseeds production level of about 21 million tonnes in 1995/96 and hopes to achieve about 21.9 million tonnes in 1996/97.

Agriculture Ministry officials said the opportunities to extend the area under oilseeds were very marginal and government proposed concentrating on increasing productivity through better technology and the timely supply of inputs to farmers.
India's demand for edible oils is highly income elastic and is likely to rise much faster than the demand for cereals with rising income levels.
A.B. Godrej, director at Godrej Soaps Ltd, said consumption in the current year was expected to grow by about four percent, and the extra consumption would be met by the extra crop.
Sood estimated India's edible oil imports in 1996/97 at 1.5 million tonnes and in 1997/98 at 1.75 million tonnes.
He estimated domestic oilseeds production in 1999-2000 would touch 30 million tonnes.
India is now second in the world in terms of oilseed area planted, but it occupies only fourth place in total oilseeds production.
The acreage under India's oilseeds crop has risen to 26 million hectares from 19 million in the last 10 years.
Indian oilseeds yields are 800-850 kg per hectare, 40 percent of the world average, industry officials said.

The Central Organisation for Oil Industry and Trade (COOIT) has told the government it should allow free oilseeds imports to get over the problem of chronic capacity under utilisation in the processing industry and to meet the edible oil shortage.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, at a convention in November, promised to look into the COOIT demand. He said the government would consider allowing free imports provided farmers were protected and consumers benefitted from the move.
Gowda said the government would also consider removing controls on the storage of oilseeds and an alteration to the tax structure.
But Shah said the import of oilseeds was not advisable.
"While importing oilseeds there will be no control on stocks and there will be hoarding," Shah said.
